tracks.show: Columbia Business School · Heilbrunn Center · Fireside chat (Oct 5, 2026)
tracks.note: Tano Santos 교수의 소개 후, Li Lu가 가치투자의 6가지 원칙을 정리해요: Ben Graham의 3가지(주식=기업 소유권, 시장은 나를 '가르치는' 게 아니라 '섬기는' 존재, 안전마진), Buffett의 능력범위(circle of competence), Munger의 '물고기가 있는 곳에서 낚시하라', 그리고 Li Lu 자신의 '부 = 세계 구매력에 대한 지분'. 시장 참여자 4가지 유형 이야기도 나와요. 1회차는 대략적인 흐름만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Thank you so much.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I know you guys are incredibly excited to be here, and I know it’s not because of me, but rather because of our guest today, who I will introduce shortly.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Before we start with the interview, let me take a couple of minutes to tell you that, as always at this time of year, the Heilbrunn year is up and running in full swing.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: The students, some of whom are here, have already taken my Modern Value class.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: They’re taking the Applied Value Investing class, their Credit Superhighway, all the electives.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: We’re having a blast.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: They’re all absolutely wonderful.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: In addition, we have a new initiative this year in the Heilbrunn Center.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: We launched our first Global Value Investor program, and the first cohort of that program, a joint effort with Columbia Business School Executive Education, is here.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: These are all the wonderful friends from China who are visiting us this year.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Thank you so much for being here.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Michael and I — I get asked this question a little too often — are already working on a new season of the Value Investing with Legends podcast.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Episodes will be coming soon, so that is something to look forward to.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: We made our new stock selections for the student portfolio, the Tom Russo student portfolio.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: What did we buy this year?

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Equifax, Humana.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: What else?

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: We bought the great Japanese bicycle company, Shimano, a classic value play if there was one; Copart, an online auction company; Perimeter Solutions, fire solutions.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: A lot of fun things.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: As always, you can download all the reports the students have done over the years on the different companies.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: It’s a wonderful resource, and I very much encourage you to look at that.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I want to single out a wonderful member of our community.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I’m always amazed by Tom Russo’s generosity with the Heilbrunn Center, not only because of the student portfolio, but because of everything he does for the program, and in particular this year, making sure that our friend Li Lu could be here, for which we’re always thankful.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: We just had a wonderful week, as I told you a moment ago.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: With this new program, the Global Value Investor program, Andrew Gundlach and Kristin Gilbertson put on a show for them, which I also want to acknowledge publicly.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Finally, we’re getting ready for a terrific CIMA conference.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: It’s amazing, the names that are coming this year.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: We’re going to have Howard Marks, Bill Ackman will be there, Josh Wolfe of Lux Capital will be there, Samantha McLemore from Patient Capital.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I very much hope to see many of you there.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Now, to the main event.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Li Lu, of course, needs no introduction, as he’s truly one of the great modern value investing legends.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: He’s the founder and chairman of Himalaya Capital, which he founded in 1997.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: He has built an enormous record of performance in the last 30 years.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Li Lu, as many of you know, is one of our most distinguished alums.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: He graduated with a law degree, an MBA degree, and a BA from Columbia College, because why get just one degree when you can get three?

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Apparently, this was how he thought about it.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: His personal story is well known.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I won’t repeat it here.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Li Lu is famous as an early investor in BYD and many of the great Chinese names, and we’ll have the opportunity to discuss issues related to the Chinese stock market today.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: First of all, Li Lu, welcome, and thank you so much for being here.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Thank you, Tano.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I’m going to talk for about 15 minutes, and then I’ll open it up for questions.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I’m going to ask you to keep them short and to the point, and I will be ruthless.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: If you take more time than I consider necessary to get your point across, I’ll cut you off and give you a nasty look.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Keep them short, because I’m sure there will be many questions.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Li Lu, I want to start here.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: As I said, you are one of the great names in modern value investing.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: You’re deeply intertwined with the story of value investing at Columbia Business School.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: We were talking about that over lunch.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: You were there at the very beginning when Bruce was launching this program.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: We know of your friendship and partnership with Charlie and Warren, and how many things you guys did together.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: We will be celebrating 30 years of the founding of Himalaya Capital next year, which is a remarkable achievement.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I want to start here.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I want you to tell us a little bit: What have you learned about value investing, and where do you think we are today?

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: What is the thing you wish you had known at the beginning?

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: What is the lesson we have now that we didn’t have when you were studying these ideas at Columbia Business School?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Thank you, Tano.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: First of all, thank you all for being here.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It is such a wonderful occasion.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Back when I was a student, as well as a young professional, I also attended a few of those luncheons.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It was the highlight.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I hope I do some justice now, 30 years later.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The discipline of value investing started with Columbia.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: When Ben Graham first started his classes, it was almost 90 years ago.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Of course, he practiced 10 or 20 years before that, so we call it a 100-year-old discipline.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It really has evolved, but some of the core principles have not and have become timeless.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If I have to distill the main principles for the discipline of value investing, I would say there are six in my mind.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Three come directly from Ben Graham, the namesake of today’s lunch; one each from Warren and Charlie; and we add a small twist — you could call that the sixth.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Here are the six basic principles in my mind that have guided our discipline, at least our practice, over the last 33 years.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Ben Graham laid it out pretty quickly as he started this discipline with three basic ideas.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: A stock is a piece of ownership, not a piece of paper to trade around.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Buying stock is really the same as buying a company.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Secondly, the market is there to serve you, not to instruct you, which is a profound insight if you are in the midst of market activities.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Thirdly, investing is about predicting the future, which is inherently unpredictable.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Therefore, you always want to require a margin of safety that will help protect the downside as well as make a better upside.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: When Warren practiced, I think he added this further discipline, which I call a circle of competence.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: All of us are probably predisposed to have certain interests, and over time you develop particular expertise and try to study more and make it better.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The most important concept of a circle of competence is knowing the edge of it, because most of us are wired to think we know a little more than we actually do.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Understanding the edge is as important as understanding what is inside it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Charlie had this idea that you’ve got to fish where the fish are.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: He was a lifelong fisherman, and that is a wonderful analogy for the actual market.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There are certain markets, industries, and businesses that draw a lot of attention.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: With that competition, your returns are averaged out.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Then there are other industries, businesses, countries, or markets that don’t attract enough attention and have far fewer fishermen.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You do way better to fish where the fish are.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It’s a simple idea, but in practice it is amazingly effective.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Lastly, over my own 33 years of practice as a global investor, applying the principles of value investing on a global basis at a time when global commerce is becoming one single market.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: One insight we have is that wealth, in the end, is really the percentage ownership of global purchasing power.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It isn’t expressed, especially in the modern economy, in the amount of gold, diamonds, or currencies of any kind.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: With inflation, all of those will dissipate over time.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What is important is what you can buy with it, what you can use it for.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: A better measurement of wealth is your percentage ownership of global purchasing power.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The way we express that is by buying great businesses in the most dynamic economies at advantageous prices, waiting long enough for value to be created over time, and sharing proportionally in the upside.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Here are the six basic ideas that I think can withstand the test of time and will serve everyone well.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I like this last point very much.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I’m already deviating from the script you and I agreed on, because I think going forward, keeping an eye on that purchasing power is going to be key if we’re not able to control inflation in the presence of these fiscal challenges.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: If we have time, we’ll come back to this.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I want to get a question in before we run out of time, for the benefit of my students in the room.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: This is my prerogative as the person asking you the questions, so we’ll get this out of the way.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Value investing as a practice has seen ups and downs.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: It’s been improving conceptually over time, with Bruce, your leadership, and many of the people in this room as well.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: What is the future of the equity analyst in the age of AI?

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Do you think we can still teach what we do at Columbia Business School going forward?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Let me answer that in two parts.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: First, what investors do, and then let’s talk about AI separately.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you look at market participants, there are basically four different kinds of people.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There are investors who stay with the company over time for value creation.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There are also people who arbitrage the rights and wrongs of market pricing.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In Ben Graham’s terms, as a realist, you buy from the pessimist and sell to the optimist.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Those are the arbitrageurs.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Then you have people who are in it mostly for speculation, mostly guessing what other people would buy or sell in a certain security.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They don’t care about either the value pricing of the security or value creation.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Then there are the brokers and market makers who facilitate all that.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Most people are not necessarily purists.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They encompass somewhat of all four.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you have indexing, it is exactly that average, in a sense.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But value investors are into getting the right pricing discovery and waiting for value creation over a period of time.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I would say Ben Graham was more of an arbitrageur, and Warren is using the arbitrage price, but mostly for value creation.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The social benefit of all different ones is also quite interesting.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Speculators, by definition, don’t stay there long enough for any of the value changes or creations, so they add up to roughly zero.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Whatever is made and lost probably adds up exactly to that.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Net to society, it is a cost to the functioning of the market.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Brokerage and market making are also a cost to the functioning of the market.

tracks.title: Li Lu at the 36th Annual Graham & Dodd Luncheon (Part 2/6)
tracks.show: Columbia Business School · Heilbrunn Center · Fireside chat (Oct 5, 2026)
tracks.note: 시장의 존재 이유(저축을 생산적인 기업으로 보내는 것)와 Buffett의 비유 'a church with a casino attached'. 제로섬 게임이냐 가치 창출이냐의 선택, 그리고 AI가 '도구(tool)'인지 '피조물(creature)'인지에 대한 Li Lu의 생각이에요.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The market exists primarily for the goal of channeling excess savings into productive use, into deserving companies, and creating this modern economy that has compound economic growth.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is why the stock market exists in the first place.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Why do you have this speculative side?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It’s part of the human condition.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Warren always describes the stock market as a church with a casino attached to it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The church is where the values are created, and the casino is almost part of the building permit, a necessary cost because of the human condition.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Four hundred years ago, when it was created, this was how you inspired the animal spirit, and 400 years later it is still doing that.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This is where you’re going to make a choice as students.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Do you want to be in the zero-sum game, or the value creation game?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s a personal choice.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: As a society, you also have a choice.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You don’t want the casino side to be so out of proportion that it overwhelms the primary objective of why the market exists in the first place.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Those are choices on the individual level as well as for society.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Over 400 years, despite all this huge boom and bust, giant waste, somehow this mechanism has survived and continued to propel society as a core function.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It is pretty miraculous, to say the least.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: For your students, it is important to make that distinction early on: What do you want to do personally?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: As a society, we should also calibrate the proportion of each.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But they coexist as part of the human condition.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Now, onto AI and the market.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s a more complex question.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: First of all, what is AI, or this wave of generative AI?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It is obviously a technology, a huge technological wave.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: As a technology, we’ve been dealing with that for the last few hundred years, ever since the Industrial Revolution.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We have wave after wave of technological change, and the disruption and creation associated with it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Through that process of creative destruction, we understand some aspects of it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But somehow we feel this wave is different.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Every wave is different, but this wave is unusually different from anything we’ve experienced so far.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What makes it so different this time?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: On the surface, you can see the pace of change, the scale involved, and the concentrated financial impact at the top, the nature of that concentrated financial impact at the top.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They’re all incredibly unprecedented.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Then you ask why that is the case.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The narrative is slightly different.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Most of the time, until this moment, we’ve been dealing with technological changes as a fundamental tool for human productivity.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: With this technology, we introduce a different element.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We now have a spectrum of tool versus creature, and we begin to change on that spectrum of tool versus creature.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The moment it was first introduced, nearly four years ago, was the moment of the Turing test.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: At that point, we could no longer tell from language whether it was a machine or a human.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: From that point on, we were introduced to reasoning, and it began to gain more and more human features.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: From reasoning comes coding.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: With coding capability, it becomes an autonomously executing agent that functions much as a human does.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Then comes the collaboration of all the agents in complex and long-lasting tasks—call that long reasoning.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Much like human society, agents would organize, self-organize, prioritize, and execute tasks in an ever more sophisticated fashion, with their own language communication tools.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s where we are.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you look at the Silicon Valley narrative, the generative AI will go to the stage of RSI, which we’re partially in – the idea that all the improvement would eventually be self-made, without a human in the loop.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: From RSI we will come to AGI, then ASI, the intelligence level exceeding all humans, individually as well as together.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: From there, you would say we’re creating somewhat of a semi-god or demigod, but a man-made creation.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Because that is so powerful and all-encompassing, the economic impact, by definition, has to be huge and therefore justify all the different investment costs.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: When you have trillion-dollar IPOs, you’re all invited to participate in the IPO of a god or something.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is the narrative, and that is what makes it different.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But if you step back and say – If this were indeed the case, what would become of humans?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We would live in a society lorded over by a man-made god, accessed by very few and understood by none.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Not even controlled – we can’t say that, because nobody understands it at that point.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Is there anyone in humanity who would like to live in that society?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: My answer is probably a resounding no.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I don’t think anyone would want to live in that society.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There are only two outcomes, in a sense.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: A) This technology is not progressing in that direction, and we can discuss what it is and why it is not; or B) If it is indeed progressing in that direction, we will all, at some point, unite together to stop it from becoming that.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In neither case are we going to have a man-made god living and lording over human society.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is what distinguishes this generation of technology, why it is different, and the different impacts, particularly the financial market impact.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But leaving that aside, when you ask – Is this a useful technology?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The answer is also a resounding yes.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What is it, in essence?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If I were to give it a provisional definition, from observing what it does and where it came from – Generative AI is a machine that by applying brute compute with clever algorithms, using all human-generated data and its first derivative, come up and establish systematic contextual correlations among near-infinite variables of human-generated data and its first derivative.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In doing so, it establishes capabilities that include much of human reasoning and human intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: At present, we know how it works and how to make it better, but we don’t quite understand why it works, much as to the extent that we don’t quite understand how human machinery works.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: With that provisional definition, observing what is happening now, it equalizes a layer of the economy that is very helpful.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you look at the economy, at the bottom we have energy and transportation.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: On top of that sits manufacturing.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: On top of that, we have communication and digital media.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Then we have an enormous amount of knowledge-based, technology-based services that synthesize all the knowledge we’ve accumulated and serve all the different layers of the economy.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Generative AI today, at its current stage, is great at synthesizing and equalizing all the knowledge and expertise that has accrued to that layer, helping all the other ones.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But it can’t change, for example, energy and transportation.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It doesn’t change manufacturing, which is essentially the combination of different molecules and atoms and transforming them into different combinations.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In communication and digitization, they’re already great synthesizers.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is the realm where it is going.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It has not gone beyond humans.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: By this extension, it may not rise to whatever the narrative would dictate or lead you to believe.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We’re still firmly within the human-generated data realm.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: To go to the biological sense requires a whole different level.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: For example, our—this may be going too far.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Go for it.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Knock yourself out.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Each cell contains let’s say at least fifty petabytes of files, and you need to multiply that by trillions to get us on the biological level.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We’re not anywhere close to getting to that level.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But what has been established already begins to tip this balance between tool versus creature.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: One of the two arguments would persuade you to stop any further development without a human in the loop.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: RSI – recursive self-improvement – without a human in the loop would be very dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They would develop goals and subgoals for their own purposes, and that would get them further from human control.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In summary, this technology is enormously helpful, transformative, and extraordinarily dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We have to, as a society and together as human beings, have a red line to firmly establish that whatever the self-learning or utilization of the tools, it cannot be without a human in the loop.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In other words, firmly establish it on the tool side rather than the creature side.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It’s also enormously disruptive, from employment to emotional dependency to risks from cyber to bio to nuclear.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the end, what you want society to develop is a balanced pace of development that balances benefit and risk.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: By the way, this technology will always have incremental costs.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This is fundamentally different from the internet or a bunch of previous technologies, where you have a one-time investment and can amortize it for a long time.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This is not the case.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You always have an incremental cost associated with it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Cost, revenue, and profit are also very important.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Capital needs and financial discipline will always be in operation.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Also, the pace of development and the level of societal tolerance.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You have four or five different layers of considerations for pacing and development into it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: How does human society adapt to those kinds of changes?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Not always by planning.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We’re going to go through big boom and bust cycles, or even multiple ones.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is the nature of how it is going to develop.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Those are the lines we have to think about as we approach this transformative, dangerous, disruptive, and costly technological wave.

tracks.title: Li Lu at the 36th Annual Graham & Dodd Luncheon (Part 3/6)
tracks.show: Columbia Business School · Heilbrunn Center · Fireside chat (Oct 5, 2026)
tracks.note: Nvidia 쏠림 시장과 AI 회사 상장 설명서의 모순(2조 달러 가치, 인류 위험 10%)을 예로 시장의 비합리성을 이야기해요. 이어서 중국 경제의 지난 10년: 중진국 함정, 2021년 부동산 정점, 가계 자산 60–70% 하락.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I think what you said, Li Lu, about this combination of being extraordinary, dangerous, and our not completely understanding why it is generating some of the answers it is generating, would require a human in the loop to check over it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Once again, it’s going to be the scarce supply of this skill, of the person monitoring the artificial intelligence output, that will determine where rents are going to be located.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s right.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: That effectively means if you’re smart and can communicate effectively with that AI inside any domain, you’re going to be the scarce resource, and probably the rents are going to accrue to you.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Do I understand this correctly?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I think that’s somewhere along those lines.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It has different aspects and nuances, but I think that’s the case in the end.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Let’s start projecting these ideas.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: One of the things that is most striking when we walk into the classroom—there are many of my colleagues here teaching capital markets, financial markets, value investing, investing in general—is that this is one peculiar market.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I have a very vague question for you.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: The market seems to be driven by a very low number of companies that are pushing the technological frontier.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: The world seems dependent on these companies to push this frontier, and as a result, valuations are completely distorted by that.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: There’s a plot I show my students: the market capitalization of the company with the highest market capitalization, normalized by GDP.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: That number traditionally has been between 2 and 4 percent.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: It is now about 15 percent with Nvidia.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: How do you think about this market, one that is becoming overly dependent on those few companies, with a very high beta to those companies?

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: How do we design portfolios to protect ourselves against the shocks of this technology?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The market always does peculiar things.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: From the very beginning, we go through this, and we’ll probably continue to do so.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You don’t have to be dictated to by what the market decides to do at any given time.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This is one of the most important insights and contributions from Ben Graham himself.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: At this point, if you look at the proposition of one recent prospectus that I read.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Here’s a company that calls itself a research lab, yet it burns through tens of billions and promises to continue burning through hundreds of billions of dollars.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It promises a transformative technology, but at the same time has a 10 percent chance of killing everyone.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It wrote that in the prospectus and invited everybody to put in at least $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If there is there any inconsistency or irony?!

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Then this is.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This is one extreme illustration of how irrational the market gets.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It cannot both be true, but that’s where they are.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It also tells you that things are not rational and not sustainable.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Eventually, they won’t continue.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Those are also the rules of the market, if you look throughout the centuries.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They do strange things over a long period of time.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Take the S&P since 2010, for example.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the last 16 years, it averaged 14 or 15 percent.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the preceding 10 years, from 2000 to 2010, it averaged exactly zero — in fact, slightly negative for 10 years.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you average the last 26 years, you get high single digits, and that is roughly right over the long term.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If GDP grew in that period maybe 2 percent, and you have 2 to 3 percent inflation, you average about 4 to 5 percent nominal growth.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Publicly listed companies do slightly better, especially those chosen by elimination to be the 500 best companies.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You come up with high single digits, and that is where the long-term average has been.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That should serve as a basic grounding pillar of getting what you deserve and how the market rationalizes over a longer period.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But it is punctuated by periods, sometimes long periods, when it goes to extremes.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The example we just cited does strike people as, at a minimum, odd.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That happens throughout history.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If we ground society in the sense that a super-creature is simply not allowed or tolerated, it won’t go there.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If it stays in the realm of tools, it will be like any other tool, with costs and benefits associated with it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Therefore, financial discipline and capital market discipline will eventually apply.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The way you get there is through multiple ups and downs and boom and bust cycles, and that’s also fine.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: From that perspective, the bifurcation as a result of it — at any given time, you don’t create an enormous amount of new capital.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If it is overwhelmingly driven to the top, that means you also have a whole bunch of otherwise wonderful businesses trading at very low prices.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This is the same here, in China, or anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In China, it is probably more extreme, as some of the Chinese participants would be well aware.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Over time, the weight of the market will dictate the long-term returns of investors.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You still get what you deserve in the end.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There’s not much of a free lunch, even if it appears to be for a period of time, even a long period.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Over the longer term, it will be weighed out by the natural weight of market rationalization itself.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s why it has existed for a few hundred years already.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I would say this bifurcation offers those with a rational mind a better opportunity set than at other times, if you stay rational, which is very difficult.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It’s easy to get swept up, especially when you have a big technology wave.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Your margin of imagination can expand dramatically.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The speculative side of the market gets much more active, and the imagination becomes wilder, so the exaggerations tend to be more extreme.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But for a rational mind, those create a better long-term opportunity set than otherwise.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: You mentioned China briefly there.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Let’s talk a little bit about that.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I just came back from China.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I was teaching the participants in Hong Kong, and I took advantage of that occasion to do a couple of cases on Chinese companies and study the Chinese market a little.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: It’s been quite a ride over the last few years.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: How do you think about the Chinese market these days, with the problems in the Chinese economy associated with the real estate bust and the banking crisis?

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: It looks reminiscent of some of the things we’ve seen in other places.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: How do you see investing in China these days?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You mentioned the Chinese market.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you look at the last 10 years, it has basically been stagnant.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What happened in those 10 years is fascinating.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Ten years ago, the Chinese government had a decision to make.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They had achieved somewhat of a middle-income level.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The question was: How do we break away from it?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: So many countries have reached that level and stagnated there, so much so that there is a term to describe it – the middle-income trap.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Dozens of countries achieved that and stayed there 40 or 50 years later.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: China is a large economy, so the question naturally is: What keeps a middle-income country stagnant and prevents it from breaking through the ceiling?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You manufacture, you industrialize, you go with mid- to low-end manufacturing, but never break away from it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They had a decision to make.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Do we want to break out, and can we do something to accelerate that process or make sure it happens?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: On its natural course, a lot of countries have failed to achieve that and stayed there for 40 or 50 years, some countries even longer.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They embarked on this process of deliberately migrating the economy from low- to mid-end manufacturing into mid- to high-end manufacturing.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Instead of a five-year plan, they had a 10- year plan called Made in China 2025, in which they listed about 10 major objectives aimed at transforming Chinese basic manufacturing from low- to mid-end into mid- to high-end.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: A few years after that started, the first Trump administration came on board and started the trade war.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This reinforced their idea that not only might they not break through that ceiling on their own natural course, but other countries might deliberately constrain them underneath it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The first Trump administration was followed by the Biden administration, which not only kept the trade tariffs but also added more technology restrictions.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Five years into the 10-year plan, by 2021, the Chinese government doubled down on that direction.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In addition to migrating manufacturing into the mid- to high-end, it added technological self- sufficiency, particularly in areas where they had real bottlenecks: semiconductors, big aircraft engines, operating software code, and so on.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There was a long list China was facing.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That started another five years of doubling down and accelerating that process.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: When you try to achieve those impossible goals that so many countries have failed to achieve, it doesn’t come without deep and heavy costs.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That has been the model by which China developed its economy.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: At different periods, they have big objectives and targets, with big costs associated with them.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You mentioned real estate.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the last five years, one of the principal costs of achieving that goal has been the balance sheets and family wealth of middle-class Chinese families.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: By 2021, real estate prices reached their peak.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: A typical middle-class Chinese family had 70 percent of its net worth tied up in the home it owned.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But that home carried roughly 50 percent leverage through a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the next five years, until now, real estate prices nationwide lost about 40 percent of their value on average.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They saw their entire family fortune go down 60 to 70 percent on average.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: When that happens, what do you do?

tracks.title: Li Lu at the 36th Annual Graham & Dodd Luncheon (Part 4/6)
tracks.show: Columbia Business School · Heilbrunn Center · Fireside chat (Oct 5, 2026)
tracks.note: 중국 가계가 한 세 가지(덜 쓰고, 더 저축하고, 빚 갚기), Made in China 2025와 '목표(objective)가 비용(cost)이 되는' 구조, 그리고 싸게 거래되는 세계적 기업들. 지난 30년간 형성된 단일 글로벌 시장 이야기예요.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You do three things: consume less, save more, and, to the extent possible, pay down debt.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is exactly what typical middle-class Chinese families have done over the last five years.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Domestic demand has been growing slower and slower, to today roughly zero.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Savings have gone up to about 120 percent of GDP, probably the largest savings deposits anywhere in the world, basically RMB 165 trillion.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: People have also been through two or three years of roughly zero price increases or slightly negative ones, more or less in that range.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Therefore, they have a bit of a confidence issue when they look to the future.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is one tier of the economy.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But if you look at the other tier, at the Chinese government’s objectives over the last 10 years and five years, you see a remarkably different picture.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Chinese manufacturing has finally broken through from low- to mid-end, firmly into mid- to high-end.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Every single objective of Made in China 2025 has been hit.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the last five years, solving the bottleneck issues has also made tremendous progress.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Take the example of semiconductors.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It turns out that the U.S.-led technology sanctions have been a godsend for the Chinese semiconductor industry because they have one of the most precious things in a market economy – DEMAND.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Ask any entrepreneur what is most important, and they say the order book.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you have revenue, you get the whole ball rolling.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: With more revenue comes profit, comes R&D, comes better improvement, comes more revenue.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That happened to the point that, on mature nodes, both the Chinese equipment side and fabrication side have achieved almost complete self- sufficiency.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: On more cutting-edge, advanced nodes, they are getting close to self-sufficiency, with a few key missing ingredients.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you keep this way, on its natural course it will happen.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s just one aspect.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: One of the key capabilities of generative AI is producing intelligence at scale on demand.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: One of the biggest applications is code generation, and that solves a big problem in some of those bottlenecks, primarily the missing layer of operating code systems.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: From PCs to servers to semiconductors to CUDA system of Nvidia, one by one, all of those are now being replaced with the help of AI.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This becomes a great equalizer.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Field after field, over the last 10 years, you’ve seen remarkable progress in migrating the basic contours of manufacturing from low- to mid-end to mid- to high-end.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In some areas—new energy, EVs, storage, batteries, you name it, and it goes on and on, heavy machinery—they dominate.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They have become global leaders.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In areas where they have bottlenecks, they have also begun to migrate and close the gap.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: At the same time, it comes with very heavy costs to other industries.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Real estate, for example, on an annual new sales basis, we’re now probably down about 70 percent.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That RMB 10 trillion is also exactly how much has been spent on manufacturing upgrading and technology efficiency, about RMB 10 trillion a year.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you look at the diversion, it is around 2021.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That has been the development model if you look back over the last 50 years of China’s development.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: At any given time, roughly every 10 years or so in my mind, you get a new set of objectives and targets, and it comes with heavy costs.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Sometimes in the next 10 years, the objective could become the cost.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the early days of industrial takeoff, the environment, air pollution, and rivers all became costs.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the proceeding next 10 years, they became the objectives, and new environmentally friendly technologies were developed.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The polluters were the cost.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the course of urbanization, real estate developers were the objective, building China into what it is, with home ownership and firm middle-class wealth.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the last five or 10 years, they became the cost.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You begin to suffer quite a bit, but overall you see the progress of the country through those periods.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is why you can compress development over a few hundred years into, say, 40 years.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But at any given time, as an investor or entrepreneur — and I’m sure all those people from China would strongly identify — you always want to know whether you are the objective or the cost.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Being the cost of a state objective is no fun!

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I’m sure all of you intimately know that or have friends involved in the process.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s how it has developed.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Overall, if you give the score, you would say that, of all those changes, you now have a country of such size and population that has finally embarked on a complete course of modernization.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But because of this two-tier economy and the general loss of confidence, you also have a financial market that has been stagnant for 10 years, going nowhere.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Meanwhile, you have some of the greatest companies, globally competitive, trading at very low prices.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Again, you have the bifurcation you see here.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you’re a rational investor and look at the whole picture, you might take a different perspective.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I would say that in today’s market, you probably find a better opportunity set than you would at different times.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s what you want.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I’m going to take questions in a moment.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: While you get your questions ready, raise your hand.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I want to ask you one last question, very quickly.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: You founded Himalaya Capital in 1997.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I arrived at the University of Chicago about the same time as a young assistant professor.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: The world, at least to me — I don’t know how it looked to you then; we didn’t know each other — was very different, or looked very different from how it looks to me now.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: It was a world that was open, transnational, where with travel you could do so many things.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: It had, I don’t know how to say it, a generosity of spirit that seems to be a little lacking today.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: It looks very different to me now.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: How do you see it going forward, and do you incorporate any of those ideas into the way you think about investing?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It’s a great question, Tano.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The world has changed over the last 30 years.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There’s no question about that.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The world order, or the big questions of how the world governs and operates itself, changes on a slow scale.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It takes decades, sometimes a hundred years, for an order to form and transform.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The current world order was founded through two great world wars, which brought the whole world to the brink of collapse.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Coming out of that, an American-led order emerged.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Through the Cold War and the end of the Cold War, it became one order.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Now it’s transforming once again into something yet to be seen, to emerge into what would emerge out of it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Underneath, there is another order that has been steadily forming for the last few hundred years: the economic order.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It forms when more and more countries and populations join in common trade and transact business with each other.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They form a common market.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That common market was finally formed roughly 30 years ago, with the collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of the Cold War.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Virtually all countries and populations began to join one market economy.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What is interesting about this economic order is that, once a common market is formed, it is very difficult for any single country to withdraw voluntarily.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Out of the market comes efficiency, comes the flywheel of continuous improvement along the lines of technology, efficiency, division of labor, trading of resources, and so on.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Any country that withdraws for an extended period would face a great deal of cost.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the end, once it is formed, it is very difficult to disintegrate.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It lasts much longer.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Look at the trade wars and trade frictions over the preceding hundred years.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: No matter what frictions and barriers you erect, people find a way to trade through a third country, along the same principles of comparative advantage.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Take U.S.–China trade.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Of course, that has declined, but if you look at overall U.S. trade with Mexico plus ASEAN, they exactly offset it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Basically, U.S.–China trade remains the same, it just goes through a third-party country.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is roughly true in most other markets as well.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In the political order, the U.S., having led the globe for 80 years and shouldered most of the costs of ensuring that the economic common market functions as it sees fit, began to realize that the costs and benefits derived from it were probably a bit out of proportion.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It began to voluntarily withdraw some of those responsibilities, not very successfully so far, leaving a vacuum.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The single biggest change in the political order is the rise of China over the last 30 or 40 years.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It has become an enormous economic entity, with a complete set of manufacturing and technological self-sufficiency, and a single largest market that is also open, with unified regulation.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is a huge change to both the political and economic orders we are witnessing.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: At the same time, our mutual dependency, with one single market, has only increased, not decreased, over that period.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I’ll give you one example.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In generative AI, the one thing everybody needs is chips, semiconductor chips.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Where are those chips being made?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Think about all the countries that produce them.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They have one thing in common.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What do you think that might be?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Sorry, I’m not putting you on the spot.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I’m perfectly on the spot.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Now I have to think about semiconductors when I was thinking that I need to open for questions.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: What do they all have in common?
