tracks.show: Columbia Business School · Heilbrunn Center · Fireside chat (Oct 5, 2026)
tracks.note: 반도체 국가들의 공통점(젓가락!), 미·중 상호의존과 전략적 안정. Berkshire가 '교회'를 대성당으로 키웠다는 비유 후 Q&A가 시작돼요: 중국 vs 미국 AI, 중국 증시, 정치 리스크.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: One thing in common among all the places that produce semiconductor chips essential for this technological wave, which the whole country seems to be betting on, is that every country and all the people who produce semiconductor chips use chopsticks.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Think about that.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Without exception.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Of course, all the people leading the semiconductor companies in this country also use chopsticks, from Jensen to Lip-bu to Lisa, you name it, Hock, all of them.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There is a great deal of mutual dependency, as you can see.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you’re betting to the extent we’re currently betting as a country and as companies on this new technology, whatever its promise and peril could be, then you have to be nice to people who use chopsticks.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This is not changing.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It didn’t happen by accident; we can go into why.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There is a reason the president of the United States and the president of China find an urgency to meet four times in eight months.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Two into it, the other two coming.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The most important accomplishment of every meeting is that we schedule the next meeting.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That comes the term strategic stability.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In other words, stability is of strategic importance.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I highlighted the sense of one global common market, the cost of withdrawing voluntarily from it, and mutual dependency deepening in a peaceful manner.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Meanwhile, everybody is competing fiercely, all believing time is on their side.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: China to complete semiconductor self-sufficiency and all kinds of other things, the U.S. hoping for a breakthrough in AI and what it can promise.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Other countries have different sets of calculations.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It all highlights that peaceful stability is of paramount importance to everyone, of strategic importance.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The largest countries have the responsibility and the desire to keep it that way.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: All countries would felt the weight of one single common market and the cost of withdrawing from it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The world, by and large, will continue to progress in that regard.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The order we have been familiar with since the end of World War II is changing and transforming.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What will emerge, and in what form, is yet to be seen.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But the underlying formation of something with a more prominent impact, the forming of one single global common market, is here to stay.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What is the implication for an investor?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We come back to our basic tenets of value investing, the six principles.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The last one we added is that, as a global investor, your wealth is expressed as your percentage ownership of global purchasing power.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: One way to accomplish that, certainly the way we’ve been practicing, is by buying great businesses in dynamic countries and markets at advantageous prices, and holding them for the long term to create value, preserve our percentage, and grow it over time.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Back to Warren’s analogy describing the stock market as a church with a casino attached to it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What Berkshire has accomplished over the last 60 years is to build that church into a gigantic cathedral, which not only symbolizes and functions, but where people can find spiritual solace, because it provides the right function for which the market exists.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What we’re trying to practice, back to your question, over the last 30 years, is that we want to prove that the gospel can be spread.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We can build churches in other countries.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We chose to build that church in Asia as well as other regions, as a global investor.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Over time, some of those churches will appear in different countries, and some might grow into cathedrals as well.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Let’s come back to your other question, to students and young professionals: What would you choose to do in this market?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This is the basic setup, a church with a casino attached as part of the permitting process because of the human condition.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They have different implications for the overall society.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: On one side, you have a win-win approach and a net benefit to society.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: On the other, you have zero-sum and a net cost, a net negative impact on society.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The choices are yours.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Technology, including AI, will remain a tool, not a replacement.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If it has any tendency to replace humans, as I said, we will all unite to oppose such a creation of a man- made god.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Therefore, in my view, you don’t have to participate in a prospectus that calls it an IPO of a demigod.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is one way to express our collective duties to a good society.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s why this program exists, and I think it ought to continue.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Thank you very much.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: We have 15 minutes for a couple of questions.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: All the way in the back—you were the first to raise your hand, so you get the right to do it.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: The only thing is that I’m going to ask you guys seriously to make it quick.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: Thank you again.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: I really appreciate it.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: I just want to get your sense of the difference between Chinese AI and American AI.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I’ll take two more questions at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I will answer all three together.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Who else were raising their hand.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: All the way in the back there.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: And someone here, too.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We’ll do three questions at a time.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: You mentioned the Chinese market.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: I want to hear your opinion about whether the Chinese stock market could be the objective or the cost.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: That’s a good question, actually.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: One more.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: I’m curious how you underwrite political risk when the rules can change overnight, considering you’ve been so successful investing in Chinese businesses.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The Chinese approach towards AI, whether the Chinese market is objective or cost, and how you underwrite political risk.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They’re all connected, of course.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you describe the Silicon Valley approach to AI, the fundamental question is: What else can this technology do?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s why they still call them research labs.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I want to see what else it can do.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: How far can we push the edge of it?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s why I also call it a frontier.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The Chinese AI companies, I would say, are fundamentally curious about those questions as well.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But in addition, and more importantly, they ask: What can this technology do for my customers, both my consumers and enterprise customers?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There lies a very different approach.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You can see from various metrics how the results will be different.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The Chinese stock market — is that the objective or cost?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: At different times, the emphasis is different.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But when you are the primary balance sheets of both individual families and the nation, when the real estate as a proportion begins to go down in one way, by the way, they don’t really go down forever because it has real value, then what in its place, would constitute the wealth of the nation, the people, and the families?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: When you answer that question, you would say that at some point, whether it’s today or another time, it has to be.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is the only asset that grows with the economy, in fact grows because of the economy, and is also the reason why the economy grows.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They are all in a flywheel together.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: On political risk, that comes to do with understanding the objective at any given time, the history, and examining the record of all of it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That doesn’t just relate to China, it relates to the U.S. and a whole bunch of different questions.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Our whole world is still somewhat organized around nation-states, and that’s the reality we live with.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: With all the considerations we talked about, we should apply that to all the countries in which we operate.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Next set of questions.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: Can you apply value investing principles and strategies to investments in growth companies or high-tech companies?

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: The tech question.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: The second question I have is about the issue of energy convergence and intellectual capital, because energy markets are now very correlated with the consumption of knowledge-based businesses.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: I’m wondering whether this has implications for solving or creating problems involving climate issues, environmental issues, and others.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: I would also love to hear any thoughts you have on crypto markets in the context of global financial conditions.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: You got three questions in one, but we will forgive you.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: I’m a Columbia alumnus and already in the church of value investing and have been practicing for two years.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: The risk of underperformance in the investment business, where you try to preach value and see things slip away, holds real career risks.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: How do you think about it?

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: That’s a wonderful question.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There are five or six questions, somewhere there.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Value investing principles and growth and technology companies; energy and all the associated implications for current AI, climate change, and somehow relating to crypto.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: You can do it, Li Lu.

tracks.title: Li Lu at the 36th Annual Graham & Dodd Luncheon (Part 6/6)
tracks.show: Columbia Business School · Heilbrunn Center · Fireside chat (Oct 5, 2026)
tracks.note: Q&A 후반: 성장주에도 가치투자를 적용할 수 있나, 크립토에 대한 짧은 답, 안전마진 확보법, 그리고 마지막 메시지 '복리의 핵심은 이미 가진 것을 잃지 않는 것'.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The third one is about underperformance and how you keep yourself in business, even though you’re two years into it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: First of all, the value principle — I put it this way.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I think all intelligent investment is value investment, because you always want to get a little more than what you pay for.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What you pay is the price; what you get is value.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Whatever value you can express yourself, whether it is in a business that is stagnant or even declining but pays you a whole bunch of money back, or a company that is rapidly growing, or a bet that has only a small percentage of winning and a large percentage of losing, therefore you spread — all of that come down to your understanding of where value will be created.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The basic principle is discounted future cash flow, to the extent that you can understand and estimate it accurately.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: They all come down to the same mathematics.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s why I say almost all intelligent investing is value investing.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The basic principle doesn’t change.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You can apply it differently based on where your circle of competence is, going back to the concept Warren articulated so well.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Energy is obviously essential, an essential layer of the economy.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I see energy and transportation, manufacturing, communication, and then knowledge-based services.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Those are essentially the entire economy.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Of course, they have applications in every single layer.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Of cause right now, the constraint on AI ranges from chips to electricity to labor.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It applies differently, and it has an impact on climate.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Any one of those subjects, we could go into almost endless aspects of it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But your third question, regarding your question about crypto, I have a very simple answer.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I don’t think anything of it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I think eventually it will disappear on its own, and that’s okay, because it’s fundamentally bogus.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you think about what constitutes a currency that is redeemable, it is enforced because of the forces associated with it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Without that mechanism of enforcement, you cannot have any enforceable measure of settlement or store of wealth.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Some guys creating it out of a garage doesn’t do the job.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Yes, it helps criminals and facilitates all kinds of illicit transactions.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I think we’re all better off banning it, but that’s okay.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If somebody wants to collect it in the same way people think a certain artist is worth a certain price, that’s your personal preference.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But as a society, I think nothing of it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It’s very simple.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Now, your question is very real.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You’re buying into it, but then, of course, you also want to ask it to cooperate with you.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: As I said, that is where human psychology is.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Everybody likes to have the best of both worlds.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In fact, they want everything – I want to be doing win-win, but I also want to report good numbers every year at least, preferably every quarter, then every month, every day, every hour – Pretty soon, you will become a speculator.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You cannot have both worlds.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Either you think the market is there to instruct you, or you think the market is there to serve you.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You can only take one of the two.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Anyone who wants to mishmash all of it is better off indexing, because it is exactly the average of all the market participants.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You average out those four kinds of market participants, that’s the index.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You’re better off doing that.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: If you say – How do I make a business out of it? – In the end, you have to have people with a like- minded approach who stick with you.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The difficult thing about this line of work is that you have to be a bit contrarian in terms of human nature.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You’ve got to have some element of a mutated genome to think you are right because logic and facts say so, not because anybody else agrees or disagrees with you.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That requires a different kind of psychology.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Some people fit it, if you decide you don’t, don’t even try.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You also have to have people who believe in that to be along with you.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Therefore, you cannot say – I want to have the biggest fund, have this AUM. – It doesn’t happen that way.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You get what you deserve in the end.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Let’s take a question from this side.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: Hi, Li Lu.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: Thanks so much for doing this.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: You’ve been such a successful investor for such a long time.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: What have you learned in the last 10 years that you think are the most important lessons that make you a better investor today than you were 10 years ago?

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: If I can sneak in a second one: You keep your mind and body very sharp at 60 years old.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: You’re taking three questions at a time and remembering all the nuances.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: I’d love to hear about your daily or weekly routines to keep your mind and body

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You got a few questions out there.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: This is like the Martha Stewart segment of the conversation, your diet and—

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Anybody else?

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: My question is about structural changes in the U.S. and Chinese capital markets.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Say that again?

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: Looking ahead a decade or more, what are the most important structural changes in the U.S. and Chinese capital markets?

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Say it in Chinese.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: I will translate.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: I’m asking about structural changes in the Chinese and U.S. capital markets.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Now I got it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I’m still struggling.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I’ll choose to understand whatever I can with my limited ability, now that I’m 60 years old.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Thank you for reminding me.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: One more.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Last one.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: When you are underwriting an investment, how do you ensure you have an adequate margin of safety and downside protection?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Where do you see the margin of safety, what have I learned in the last 10 years and how do I keep engaged this far, and structural changes between the U.S. and Chinese markets?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I don’t know what that means, but I will say something along those lines.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: One of the distinguishing characteristics that separates a value investor from most other investors is the enormous attention paid to downside protection.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Investing is predicting the future, which is inherently unpredictable.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What you do is invest in the things you do know.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What you know could be limited.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Everybody starts with very limited known knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s how I started when I was in my 20s.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I didn’t know much.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I go with the things I know are there.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The balance sheet, obviously, as in Benjamin Graham’s work, because some things are easier to understand.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Then I gradually progress from something simple to something less simple and more complex.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It’s a natural progression in terms of the circle of competence.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: About circle of competence, one thing is to understand its edge.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The other is consciously to expand it gradually over time.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I always say, if you can compound your knowledge sustainably, eventually you can compound your capital as well.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That goes back to your question about what I’ve learned over 10 years.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Every 10 years, I find I’ve learned so much that you’re almost somewhat a different person.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You want to have that renewed sense that, over a long period, if you do the right thing in the right way, it will be remarkable to find that you actually compound.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This is another reason, I would say, if you want to choose to go to a win-win situation rather than zero-sum.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You actually will compound your ability and knowledge, and perhaps your health, too.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Maybe not quite, but you can at least prolong your productive span, your health span.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Maybe not lifespan, but your health span.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You keep engaged.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It’s interesting.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You know it’s helpful to society, and you’re not taking away from society.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: With the zero-sum game, the trouble is that a lot of human nature goes to zero-sum, to the short term.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Whatever you learn today is useless tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You don’t accumulate.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You rely more and more on the impersonal.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You get a bigger computer, and now you use AI.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You’ll be replaced at some point, so what is the value of that as a human?

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Of course, I like the human in the loop.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I advocate learning, having an engaged and improved life over time, and compounding your knowledge as well as the capital of the people in the trusting way.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: What my mentor, partner, and teacher Charlie Munger always said and advocated is that the highest order of relationship he could discover is a seamless web of deserved trust.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: A seamless web of deserved trust!

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There lies a whole philosophy of approaching life in a productive way that is win-win for society as well.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I recommend anyone starting your career to lean towards that way of life.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It could take years.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: It could be slow, but slowly and surely you will get to where you deserve to go.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That is a better way of living.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Some people have a little more luck than others along the way.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Our life, success, and failure are sometimes a combination of lucky or unlucky breaks in life.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We’ve had a fair share of all of it.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: I, for one, never felt our record was completely our genius or anything.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: We’ve got so many lucky breaks along the way.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: But if you choose the right partners, the right approach, the right people to bet on, and the right things to do, over time it’s remarkable how compound returns work.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: The basic idea of compounding is that you don’t lose what you already have.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That’s a profound idea.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You don’t lose what you already have, including your knowledge, your trusting relationships, your wisdom, and even your health.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Those are amazingly powerful things to have in life.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In that regard, I think structurally the U.S. and China are the same.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: In fact, that’s the structure of humanity.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: That doesn’t necessarily answer your question, I’m sure.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Maybe we’ll find another time to discuss exactly what you mean by structural changes.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: There are always changes in life.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: This is one constant we’re always going to have to deal with.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: You will always have your share of luck and unluck, and your share of great opportunities, no matter which way you naturally lean.

transcript.speaker: Li Lu
transcript.text: Finding something you naturally lean towards and building on it over time in a compounded and cumulative fashion is just a better way of living a productive life.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: Thank you so much, Li Lu.

transcript.speaker: Tano Santos
transcript.text: This was wonderful!

listening.task: 오늘부터 출근길 듣기는 투자 거장의 실제 강연이에요. Li Lu가 Columbia Business School의 제36회 Graham & Dodd Luncheon(2026년 10월 5일)에서 한 대담 전체(약 88분)를 6개 파트로 나눴어요. 출근길에 Part 1–2, 퇴근길에 Part 3–4, Part 5–6은 시간 날 때 이어서 들어요. 어려우면 Part 1만 들어도 충분해요. 'a piece of ownership', 'margin of safety', 'circle of competence', 'fish where the fish are'가 나오는 부분을 잘 들어 보세요. 스크립트는 Columbia가 공개한 공식 녹취록(가볍게 다듬은 버전)이라 실제 말과 조금 다를 수 있어요.

quiz.q: In Part 1, Li Lu lists six principles of value investing. Which one does he credit to Charlie Munger? a) circle of competence, b) margin of safety, c) fish where the fish are
quiz.answer: c) fish where the fish are. 평생 낚시꾼이었던 Munger의 비유로, 관심이 몰린 시장은 경쟁 때문에 수익이 평균으로 수렴하니 '낚시꾼이 적은 곳'에서 찾으라는 뜻이에요. a)는 Buffett, b)는 Ben Graham의 원칙이에요.

reading.title: Are some salts healthier than others?
reading.source: The Economist (public reprint via Hindustan Times)
reading.summaryKo: 핑크 히말라야 소금, 플뢰르 드 셀 같은 비싼 소금도 결국 대부분 염화나트륨이라, 미량 미네랄로 건강 효과를 보려면 하루 30g 이상(WHO 권장량의 6배) 먹어야 한대요. 의미 있는 첨가물은 두 가지뿐: 아이·임산부에게 중요한 요오드(iodine), 그리고 나트륨 일부를 대체하는 칼륨(potassium). 중국 농촌 약 2만 1천 명 연구에서 칼륨 강화 소금(나트륨 75% + 칼륨 25%)이 혈압을 낮추고 뇌졸중·심혈관 사건·사망 위험을 약 13% 줄였어요. 그래도 가장 간단한 방법은 소금을 덜 먹는 것이고, 신장질환이 있으면 칼륨 과다에 주의해야 한대요. 검사실에서 Na/K 수치를 보는 입장에서 읽으면 더 재미있을 거예요.
excerpt: HUMANS NEED salt. It contains sodium, which draws water out of cells to hydrate the bloodstream; enables muscles to contract and relax; and helps the intestines absorb nutrients. But one can have too much of a good thing.
Despite their differing appearances and price points, most supermarket salts—from fleur de sel to pink Himalayan—predominantly consist of plain old sodium chloride.
reading.tip: Economist는 말장난을 좋아해요: 'more than a grain of truth'(일리가 있다), 'taken with a pinch of salt'(곧이곧대로 믿지 않다), 'worth their salt'(제 몫을 하는) 모두 소금(salt/grain/pinch)과 관련된 관용구예요. 하나씩 찾아보세요!
